references.text: Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt—an example warning against looking back after being called out, paralleling Jesus' warning about looking back after putting one's hand to the plow.

Elijah called Elisha while he was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen. Elisha asked to say farewell to his parents but then followed Elijah without looking back—a direct background for Jesus' words about putting one's hand to the plow.
Proverbs warns against those who are unstable in their ways. Looking back after beginning to plow shows such instability that it makes one unfit for God's kingdom.
Paul describes forgetting what lies behind and straining forward toward what is ahead, toward the goal—the same attitude Jesus requires of anyone who wishes to follow him without looking back.
Hebrews warns about those who have tasted the heavenly gift yet fall away—a serious parallel to beginning to follow Jesus but then looking back.
"The righteous shall live by faith, but if he draws back, my soul has no pleasure in him." Looking back from the plow is precisely drawing back, which stands in opposition to faith.
Peter warns that for those who have known the way of righteousness but turn away, the last state becomes worse than the first—the image of looking back after beginning to follow Christ.
The immediate context where Jesus meets several who wish to follow him but with conditions—to bury his father or say farewell to those at home—shows that unconditional discipleship is required.
Jesus speaks of the cost of being a disciple: whoever does not carry their cross and follow him cannot be his disciple. Half-hearted discipleship makes one unfit for God's kingdom.
Jesus warns against turning back to get one's belongings, reminding them of Lot's wife—the same principle of not looking back once one has begun to follow God's call.
